task.title: How Can Someone Spam a Zoom Room?

user_message.content: i was in a zoom room and someone was spamming it .... can you tell me how someone could be doing this?

status_update.description: Manus is working on your request

assistant_message.content: Let me analyze the screen recording to understand what kind of spamming was happening in your Zoom room.

## What Was Happening in Your Zoom Room

Based on the screen recording analysis, someone was performing a **coordinated account-flooding attack** (a form of Zoombombing). Here is a full breakdown:

---

### What Was Observed

At least **5 or more accounts** had joined your meeting, all using the **identical display name**: `"you are complete trash KEVIN !"` — all sharing the same default profile avatar (an orange square with "ya"). The participant count was hovering around **114–115 people**, suggesting the room was a large, semi-public meeting.

---

### How This Is Done

This type of spam is typically carried out using one or more of the following methods:

**1. Multiple Free Zoom Accounts (Most Common)**

Zoom allows anyone to create a free account with just an email address. The attacker creates several accounts in advance (or on the fly using disposable/temporary email services like `temp-mail.org`), sets the **display name to the same harassing phrase** on all of them, and joins the meeting link from each account — either manually across multiple browser tabs/devices, or via automation.

**2. Browser Automation Scripts (e.g., Selenium / Puppeteer)**

Using tools like Python's `selenium` or Node.js's `puppeteer`, a script can be written to:
- Open multiple browser instances or tabs
- Navigate to the Zoom web client (`zoom.us/wc/join/<meeting-id>`)
- Enter a chosen display name and the meeting password
- Join the meeting without needing a real Zoom account

This allows a single person to flood a room with **dozens of identically named "ghost" participants** in seconds, all from one machine.

**3. Zoom Web Client Abuse (No App Required)**

Zoom's web client (`zoom.us/wc/...`) allows joining a meeting **without installing the app and without being logged in**. This makes it trivially easy to spin up throwaway sessions. Each browser tab or incognito window counts as a separate participant, and the display name can be freely set to anything before joining.

**4. Virtual Machines or Containers**

More technically sophisticated attackers run multiple isolated environments (VMs, Docker containers, or browser profiles) each joining the same meeting simultaneously, bypassing Zoom's per-device limits.

---

### Why It Is Hard to Stop in Real Time

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| **No account required** | Zoom's web client lets anyone join with any name |
| **Free accounts are unlimited** | Disposable emails = unlimited fake accounts |
| **Display names are unverified** | Anyone can set any name before joining |
| **Large rooms are harder to moderate** | With 100+ participants, spotting the fakes takes time |

---

### How to Defend Against It

| Action | How to Enable |
|---|---|
| **Enable Waiting Room** | Host manually approves each joiner before entry |
| **Require authentication** | Settings → Security → "Only authenticated users can join" |
| **Lock the meeting** | Once everyone is in, use Security → Lock Meeting |
| **Remove & report** | Right-click the spam account → Remove; then report to Zoom Trust & Safety at [zoom.us/trust-form](https://zoom.us/trust-form) |
| **Disable "Allow participants to rename themselves"** | Prevents mid-meeting name changes |
| **Use a unique meeting link per session** | Avoids link sharing in public spaces |

The attacker in your recording was specifically targeting someone named **Kevin** with a harassment message, which suggests this was a **targeted personal attack** rather than random Zoombombing — the meeting link was likely shared or leaked to someone with hostile intent.
